EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  

Method: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with an interaction (triple-difference) between industry-specific shocks and the time-varying cost-of-credit spread.  

Rationale:  
• The main hypotheses compare merger activity in industries that experience plausibly exogenous regulatory / technological / economic shocks with otherwise similar industries that are not shocked, before vs. after the shock date.  
• The credit-spread proxy varies only by year. Interacting it with the DiD indicator lets us ask whether “treated‐post” industries see more mergers precisely in years when external finance is relatively cheap (low spread).  
• The 1981-2000 panel (48 industries × 20 years) is well-suited for DiD; shocks arrive at different dates to different industries (staggered adoption), enabling identification from within-year cross-industry variation after absorbing year FEs.  
• We will estimate an event-study version to visualize dynamics and test the parallel-trends assumption.  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
TREAT_it = 1 if industry i is exposed to a major, well-documented shock in or before year t, 0 otherwise.  
• Shocks are coded from hand-collected chronologies: e.g., 1984 AT&T break-up (Telecom), 1986 and 1992 Natural-Gas price deregulations (Utilities–Gas), 1994 Interstate Banking and 1999 GLB (Commercial Banks), 1996 Telecom Act (Telecom/Cable), 1980 Motor Carrier Act (Trucking), 1985–87 Oil decontrol (Petroleum & Nat. Gas), etc.  
• An industry can receive at most one “first” shock; once shocked, TREAT_it stays 1 (“absorbing treatment”).  

Control group  
Industries not yet shocked in year t form the counterfactual. Because year fixed effects absorb macro factors, identification is from within-year differences between newly shocked and still-unshocked industries.  

Treatment timing / event date  
POST_it = 1 for all years τ ≥ shock year s_i; 0 otherwise.  

Capital-Liquidity moderator  
LIQ_t = − (C&I loan rate – Fed Funds rate), demeaned. Higher LIQ_t ⇒ easier credit.  
Main regressor: TREAT_it × POST_it × LIQ_t  

No RDD is used, so no running variable.  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Parallel Trends: Absent the shock, shocked industries’ merger propensity would have evolved like non-shocked industries (after controlling for industry and year FEs). Plausible because shocks are policy or technology driven—not triggered by contemporaneous merger activity. Will be probed with pre-trend coefficients in an event study.  

A2. Exogeneity of Shock Timing: Regulatory enactment dates and exogenous technology breakthroughs are not chosen in response to impending merger plans. Historical narratives support plausibility.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (No Spillovers): Merger activity in an untreated industry is not directly affected by another industry’s shock, conditional on year FEs. Some horizontal spillovers are possible (e.g., suppliers/customers), but industry definitions minimize overlap. We will perform sensitivity tests dropping potentially linked industries.  

A4. Credit-Spread Exogeneity to Individual Industries: The aggregate spread is driven by monetary conditions and banking competition, not by one industry’s merger demand. With 48 industries, reverse causality is negligible.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  

T1. Differential Pre-Trends (violation of A1)  
• Graph and estimate event-study coefficients (−5 to −1 years).  
• Implement Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) DiD estimator that allows for staggered treatment and heterogeneous effects.  
• Re-weight the sample by propensity scores based on pre-shock observables.  

T2. Concurrent Unobserved Industry Shocks Unrelated to Regulation/Tech (omitted variables)  
• Include time-varying industry controls listed in the data description (cash-flow margin, R&D, etc.).  
• Add industry-specific linear trends.  
• Conduct placebo tests using “false” shock dates randomly assigned within ±3 years.  

T3. Endogenous Definition of Shock Exposure  
• Use external regulatory classifications (Federal Register, FCC dockets, FERC orders) rather than outcomes to code exposure.  
• Show results unchanged when redefining treatment using narrower SIC-4 or broader 2-digit groupings.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data
library(fixest)         # TWFE & CS DID
library(did)            # Callaway-Sant’Anna
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
ind <- fread("industry_year_panel.csv")   # one row per industry-year

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------------
# a) Merger intensity: number of deals ≥$50m relative to industry firms
ind[, mergers_rate := mergers_count / num_firms]

# b) Treatment indicators (already coded in CSV or add here)
# Suppose "shock_year" is in data (NA if never shocked).
ind[, treat := !is.na(shock_year)]
ind[, post  := ifelse(year >= shock_year, 1, 0)]
ind[, treat_post := treat * post]

# c) Capital liquidity (spread) – lower spread => easier credit
ind[, liq := -(ci_loan_rate - fed_funds_rate)]
ind[, liq_std := scale(liq)]  # standardize

# d) Triple interaction
ind[, triple := treat_post * liq_std]

# 3. Baseline TWFE regression ----------------------------------------------
feols(mergers_rate ~ treat_post * liq_std + 
                    cash_flow_margin + asset_turnover + r_and_d +
                    capex + sales_growth + employee_growth +
                    i(year) | industry + year, 
      data = ind, 
      cluster = ~industry) -> m1
summary(m1)

# 4. Event-study using interacted leads/lags -------------------------------
# Rel. year to shock
ind[, rel_year := year - shock_year]
ind[, leadlag := factor(rel_year)]
est_event <- feols(mergers_rate ~ i(rel_year, treat==1, ref=-1)*liq_std +
                              controls |
                              industry + year,
                   data = ind[rel_year > -6 & rel_year < 7],
                   cluster = ~industry)
iplot(est_event, ci=TRUE) + theme_bw()

# 5. Callaway–Sant’Anna DID estimator --------------------------------------
did_cs <- att_gt(yname = "mergers_rate",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "industry",
                 gname = "shock_year",        # first treatment year
                 xformla = ~ cash_flow_margin + asset_turnover + r_and_d,
                 data = ind)
aggte_cs <- aggte(did_cs, type = "group")
summary(aggte_cs)

# 6. Robustness: drop industries with potential spillovers ------------------
core_ind <- ind[!(industry %in% c("Steel", "Auto Suppliers"))]
feols(mergers_rate ~ treat_post * liq_std + controls | industry + year,
      data = core_ind, cluster = ~industry)

```

----------------------------------------------------------------  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Theory predicts that industry shocks create a “need” for reallocation, but actual merger waves only materialize when external finance is relatively cheap.  
• Direction: β_triple < 0 in the spread form (because lower spreads / higher LIQ boost mergers).  
• Magnitude (back-of-envelope): Moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of LIQ (≈200 bp change) after a shock should raise the annual merger rate by roughly 0.7–1.0 percentage points of industry firms (≈35–50% of its unconditional mean of ~2%).  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DiD)  

C1: No anticipatory effects (parallel leads) ............. 0.8  
C2: Parallel pre-trends (visual/event-study) ............. 0.7  
C3: No interference/spillovers (SUTVA) ................... 0.6  
C4: Correct functional form / no dynamics bias ........... 0.7  
C5: Robust standard errors & multiple estimators ......... 1.0  

Overall: 3.8 / 5 – credible but requires the planned robustness checks.
